chapter_title: Resilience Patterns: Circuit Breaker and Bulkhead

screens.title: Resilience Patterns: Circuit Breaker and Bulkhead
screens.subtitle: Isolate failures, prevent cascades, and keep services available

narration.text: Distributed systems require planning for failure. In this lesson you will learn the practical patterns that contain and mitigate failures so one bad component does not topple the whole system. We begin by accepting a simple truth: in a networked system, failures are not rare exceptions but expected events. The Circuit Breaker pattern protects a caller from repeatedly invoking a failing remote service, giving that remote service time to recover and reducing wasted resources. The Bulkhead pattern isolates resources so that slowness or failures in one integration cannot exhaust shared capacity. You will hear a working example in Java that shows a protected method and a fallback, and then a conceptual activity where you apply circuit breaker logic to an OrderService calling an unreliable ShippingService. We will also highlight common misconfigurations and practical tuning advice so these patterns behave as intended rather than causing false alarms. By the end, you will be able to choose, configure, and combine these patterns to improve availability and keep your microservices resilient. Consider how your current services would behave under repeated timeouts — that reflection will guide your design.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Use Circuit Breaker to avoid repeated failed calls and Bulkhead to isolate resource consumption, together preventing cascading failures.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Resilience Patterns
Resilience Patterns
Circuit Breaker and Bulkhead for microservices

This chapter shows why failures must be anticipated, how to stop cascades, and how to keep services available using two complementary patterns. Expect clear analogies, an annotated code example, and a practical activity you can follow conceptually.

In this lesson
Circuit Breaker
States, fallback, and a Java example demonstrating Resilience4j usage.
Bulkhead
Resource isolation using thread pools or connection limits to stop resource exhaustion.
Practical Steps
How to apply patterns to an OrderService/ShippingService interaction.
Quick takeaway
Design to contain failures rather than to prevent every failure. Use circuit breakers to stop repeated calls and bulkheads to isolate resources.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Visual Concept
Domino effect
A single failure can trigger dependent failures if not contained.
Circuit breaker
Stops calls to failing systems to avoid waste.
Bulkhead
Limits resource impact to a compartment.
Explore Key Topics
Circuit
Three states that protect callers and enable recovery checks.
Bulkhead
Separate pools or limits so a slow dependency doesn't starve others.
Fallbacks
Planned degraded behavior while the failing service recovers.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why resilience matters, describe how cascading failures spread, and apply two practical patterns to protect microservices. First, you will understand resilience as the system's ability to keep functioning, possibly in degraded fashion, when components fail. A concrete example is a web storefront where a slow payment provider should not stop order placement entirely. Second, you will explain the Circuit Breaker pattern: how it detects repeated failures and temporarily blocks calls so downstream systems can recover. You will see a code example that shows a protected method and a fallback that queues work or returns a user-friendly error. Third, you will describe the Bulkhead pattern: how to partition threads or connections so one slow dependency cannot exhaust shared resources. For example, creating a dedicated thread pool for email sends prevents slow email retries from blocking order processing. Finally, you will apply both patterns in a design exercise for an OrderService calling an unreliable ShippingService, writing the state actions and a simple fallback plan. These skills help you design systems that fail gracefully, monitor effectively, and reduce blast radius during incidents.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Applied View
screens.subtitle: How you'll use each skill in practice

narration.text: This second objectives slide frames each skill as an applied habit. First, when we say you will understand resilience, that means you can identify points of fragility and propose containment measures. For example, if a cache miss spikes requests to a database, resilience thinking suggests adding limits or retries rather than letting latency escalate. Second, explaining the circuit breaker means you can name its three states and prescribe actions in each: when to open, when to sample in half-open, and what a sensible timeout looks like. You will also be able to explain fallback choices such as returning cached data or queueing work for later. Third, for bulkheads you will design capacity partitions — separate thread pools, connection limits, or queue slots — and justify sizing decisions based on expected load. Finally, applying these patterns combines detection, containment, and graceful degradation. A practical checkpoint is that you can map a failure scenario to Circuit Breaker, Bulkhead, or both, and prepare monitoring that surfaces when a pattern trips. Practice this mapping as you read the upcoming examples so you can quickly pick the right containment strategy in real incidents.

screens.title: Why failures are expected in distributed systems
screens.subtitle: Designing for failure is a practical necessity, not paranoia

narration.text: Start by changing your mental model: treat failures as normal events rather than rare surprises. A distributed system spans networks, machines, and services that each have independent failure modes: transient network partitioning, degraded database performance, or a third-party A P I outage. When a component slows or fails, naive callers keep retrying and consuming resources. Over time this increases load elsewhere and can cause a cascade. A concrete example: an auth service that times out causes higher request latency across many front-end services because each waits for the auth response. If those front-end services are not protected, their threads or connections fill up and user-facing endpoints degrade or fail. The key defensive idea is containment: add layers that detect unsuccessful operations and either stop them or degrade behavior gracefully. Containment reduces blast radius by limiting how far a failure can propagate. A common misconception is that only fixing the failing service matters; while fixing root causes is essential, containment buys you time to respond and prevents immediate customer impact. Ask yourself: which dependencies could cause a cascade, and where can you place limits or fallbacks to reduce damage?

keyIdea.title: Contain failures
keyIdea.text: Expect failures and design boundaries that stop them from cascading across services and resources.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Why failures are expected
Definition
Failure as normal

Distributed systems combine many moving parts. Each can fail independently and transiently. Treating failures as expected lets you design protections such as timeouts, retries with backoff, and containment patterns like circuit breakers and bulkheads.

Concrete example
An auth service times out. Front-end services keep waiting and exhaust threads, causing user-facing endpoints to degrade. Containment prevents the problem from cascading.
Common misconception
Assuming only fixing the failing component is enough. Without containment, failures immediately affect other services while you investigate.
Key Takeaway

Design boundaries and limits to prevent a single failure from consuming system-wide resources.

Why it matters
Containment reduces mean time to recovery and limits user impact. It gives operators time to fix the root cause rather than fighting a growing pile of overloaded services.
Practical checklist
  • Identify critical external dependencies and their failure modes.
  • Add timeouts and retry policies with backoff.
  • Introduce containment patterns where repeated failures would cause resource exhaustion.
Reflection
Which single dependency in your system would cause the largest cascade if it slowed? Design one short containment you could add today.

screens.title: Cascading failure: the domino effect
screens.subtitle: How retries and resource exhaustion create a chain reaction

narration.text: A cascading failure begins with one component degrading and other services reacting in ways that amplify the problem. Picture a slow service that causes callers to wait. Those callers may use up threads, database connections, or network sockets while waiting. When resources are exhausted, additional requests fail or queue, increasing latency further. Retries without suitable backoff make matters worse by sending more traffic to the still-slow service. A concrete scenario: ProductService returns intermittent HTTP 500 errors. CatalogService keeps retrying and opens many connections. The increased load slows ProductService more, and eventually CatalogService's thread pool and connection pool are depleted, producing user-visible outages across the storefront. To interrupt the chain, add limits and detection: timeouts stop waiting indefinitely, circuit breakers stop repeated calls after a threshold, and bulkheads prevent one integration from consuming all resources. A common misconception is that increasing pool sizes solves the problem; it usually only delays the failure and increases blast radius. The takeaway: stop the loop, not just the queue. Ask: what will stop retries from amplifying the initial failure in your architecture? Cascading failure: the domino effect means prevent request amplification with timeouts, circuit breakers, and resource partitions so a single failure doesn't snowball.. In practical terms, how retries and resource exhaustion create a chain reaction. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Interrupt the loop
keyIdea.text: Prevent request amplification with timeouts, circuit breakers, and resource partitions so a single failure doesn't snowball.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Cascading failure
Process steps
  1. One service slows or fails (eg. ProductService returns 500s).
  2. Callers retry or wait, consuming threads and connections.
  3. Resource pressure slows more services, increasing failures.
  4. Without containment the problem cascades across services.
Concrete example
CatalogService keeps retrying ProductService, exhausting its thread pool and causing the storefront to return errors to users.
Containment options
Timeouts & retries
Set sensible timeouts and exponential backoff to avoid immediate retry storms.
Circuit Breaker
Stop calling a failing service after a threshold of errors to break the cascade.
Bulkhead
Isolate resource pools so one slow dependency can't exhaust global capacity.
Common mistake

Increasing pool sizes without containment only delays failure and increases blast radius.

screens.title: Circuit Breaker pattern
screens.subtitle: Stop repeated attempts to a failing service and allow recovery

narration.text: The Circuit Breaker pattern prevents a caller from continuously invoking a failing remote service. Think of it like a household circuit breaker: when an overload or short occurs, the breaker trips to protect the wiring. In software, when repeated calls to a dependency fail or time out beyond a configured threshold, the circuit opens and subsequent calls immediately fail or route to a fallback instead of attempting the remote call. This protects the calling service from wasted C P U, threads, and network resources while giving the failing service time to recover. A concrete example: OrderService calls PaymentService and sees many timeouts. A circuit breaker opens and OrderService returns a fallback response so the system doesn't keep retrying. A common misconception is that an open circuit hides problems; it does not replace fixing the failing component. Rather, it minimizes additional system harm while you repair. Use monitoring to detect open events and to trigger operator investigation. The pattern is most useful when paired with a meaningful fallback: cached data, an offline queue, or a user-friendly error that preserves system integrity while preserving the user's trust.

keyIdea.title: Circuit breaker core
keyIdea.text: Detect failure patterns, open the circuit to stop calls, test with limited requests, then close if healthy.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Circuit Breaker
What it is
Circuit Breaker

A protection mechanism that stops calls to failing services after repeated errors, returning a fallback or error immediately.

Practical example
If PaymentService times out frequently, the OrderService circuit trips and uses a fallback that queues payment for later processing.
Important elements
  • Failure detection threshold: how many failures before opening the circuit.
  • Timeout: how long to wait for a response before considering it a failure.
  • Reset timeout: how long to wait before trying test requests in half-open.
  • Fallback: what to return when the circuit is open.
Misconception check
An overly aggressive threshold creates false positives; overly lenient thresholds delay protection. Tune based on real error and latency patterns.

screens.title: Circuit Breaker states: Closed, Open, Half-Open
screens.subtitle: How state transitions protect callers and enable recovery checks

narration.text: A circuit breaker transitions between three states to balance protection and recovery checks. In Closed state requests flow normally. The breaker monitors failures and, when they exceed a configured threshold, switches to Open. In Open state the breaker immediately rejects requests or routes them to a fallback, preventing wasted calls while the dependency recovers. After a configurable timeout, the breaker moves to Half-Open. In Half-Open it allows a limited number of test requests to the dependency. If those succeed, the breaker returns to Closed; if they fail, it re-opens. Concrete example: a payment A P I that returned errors five times in a minute could cause the breaker to open for thirty seconds. During those thirty seconds order requests receive an immediate fallback response or are queued. After thirty seconds, three test requests are allowed. If two of three succeed, the circuit closes. A common misconception is expecting instant recovery as soon as the dependency is patched; in reality the Half-Open stage tests behavior under real load and prevents flapping. The takeaway: choose thresholds and sampling limits that reflect realistic error rates to avoid oscillation between states.

keyIdea.title: State machine
keyIdea.text: Closed monitors; Open stops calls; Half-Open samples to confirm recovery before fully restoring traffic.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Circuit Breaker States
Closed
Normal operation. Requests pass through and failures are counted. Transition to Open when threshold is exceeded.
Open
Requests are rejected immediately or sent to fallback. After a timeout, move to Half-Open to test recovery.
Half-Open
Allow limited test requests. If they succeed, close the circuit; if they fail, re-open.
Example walkthrough
Failure count reaches 5 in 1 minute → circuit opens for 30 seconds → after 30s allow 3 test requests → if 2 of 3 succeed, transition to Closed; otherwise back to Open.
Misconception check

Don't set very short open timeouts; you may flood the dependency during Half-Open if it hasn't recovered. Tune based on observed recovery behaviour.

screens.title: Circuit Breaker in code (Resilience4j example)
screens.subtitle: Annotated Java example with a fallback method

narration.text: Seeing circuit breaker code helps ground the concept. The chapter includes a Java example using Resilience4j that annotates a method with a circuit breaker and a fallback. In the example, a PaymentClient method attempts to call an external payment A P I. Random failures simulate service unreliability. When failures exceed the configured threshold, Resilience4j opens the circuit and subsequent calls invoke a fallback method that logs the error and returns a friendly message or queues the payment for retry. This demonstrates two important practical behaviors: the circuit prevents resource waste by stopping calls, and the fallback provides an immediate, safe alternative response. A common misconception is to return vague errors in the fallback; instead, make the fallback meaningful — queue for retry, return cached data, or provide a clear user message. When you read the snippet, notice how the fallback signature matches the original method and how exceptions are handled. Use metrics from your circuit library to emit events when the circuit opens so operators can act. Would this fallback be sufficient for your service's reliability goals, or does it need an asynchronous retry mechanism? Reflect on that trade-off.

keyIdea.title: Implementation insight
keyIdea.text: Circuit breakers integrate with fallbacks; choose fallbacks that preserve system integrity and provide recovery paths.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Resilience4j Example
Code
<!-- Java snippet from chapter, escaped for HTML -->
import io.github.resilience4j.circuitbreaker.annotation.CircuitBreaker;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class PaymentClient {

    private static final String PAYMENT_SERVICE = "paymentService";

    @CircuitBreaker(name = PAYMENT_SERVICE, fallbackMethod = "fallbackForProcessPayment")
    public String processPayment(String orderId, double amount) {
        // Simulate a call to an external payment service
        System.out.println("Attempting to process payment for order: " + orderId);
        // This call might fail or timeout
        // For demonstration, let's simulate a failure sometimes
        if (Math.random() > 0.7) { // 30% chance of failure
            throw new RuntimeException("Payment service unavailable!");
        }
        return "Payment processed for " + orderId;
    }

    private String fallbackForProcessPayment(String orderId, double amount, Throwable t) {
        System.out.println("Fallback triggered for payment for order: " + orderId + ". Reason: " + t.getMessage());
        // Log the error, potentially queue the payment for retry, or return a default error
        return "Payment failed, please try again later.";
    }
}
Explanation
  • The annotation ties a circuit to the method and specifies a fallback method.
  • On repeated failures, Resilience4j opens the circuit and calls the fallback immediately.
  • The fallback logs the reason and provides an alternative response, such as queuing the payment.
Concrete guidance
Ensure the fallback performs safe, finite actions — e.g., enqueue work or return a helpful message, not an unbounded retry loop.
Misconfiguration risk

Using a fallback that itself depends on the same failing service can reintroduce failure; build fallbacks with independent paths.

screens.title: Fallback strategies
screens.subtitle: Choosing a meaningful fallback for the caller

narration.text: Fallbacks are the planned degraded behaviors you present when a circuit is open or a call fails. Choosing the right fallback depends on the business context and safety requirements. Common options include returning cached or stale data, queueing the request for later processing, returning an informative error that preserves user trust, or using a simplified, local alternative. For example, if ShippingService is down, the OrderService might return cached shipping estimates or queue the shipping rate lookup and allow order placement with a note that rates will be confirmed later. A common misconception is to use a generic error for everything; that loses an opportunity to preserve functionality and user trust. Another mistake is making the fallback call the same failing dependency, which defeats the containment. When designing fallbacks, ensure they are independent of the failing path and that they do not create unbounded work. Also instrument fallback usage so you can measure how often users see degraded behavior and assess whether a permanent fix is needed. The takeaway: design fallbacks to preserve critical functionality while being safe and observable. Fallback strategies means prefer fallbacks that preserve functionality and use independent resources; instrument their usage to inform fixes.. In practical terms, choosing a meaningful fallback for the caller. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Fallback selection
keyIdea.text: Prefer fallbacks that preserve functionality and use independent resources; instrument their usage to inform fixes.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Fallback Strategies
Fallback options
  • Return cached or stale data with a freshness note.
  • Queue the request for asynchronous retry and return immediate acknowledgement.
  • Return a user-friendly error explaining degradation and next steps.
  • Use a local simplified logic that does not call the failing dependency.
Concrete example
When ShippingService fails, OrderService can accept the order using a cached shipping estimate and enqueue the real rate calculation. Inform the user rates will be confirmed later.
Design rules
Make fallbacks independent of the failing dependency, bound their resource usage, and instrument to know how often they run.
Misconception check

Don't use a fallback that re-invokes the same failing path or creates unlimited background work. Both defeat containment and can worsen outages.

screens.title: Tuning and common mistakes for circuit breakers
screens.subtitle: Choosing thresholds, timeouts, and half-open sampling correctly

narration.text: Circuit breakers need thoughtful configuration. Key settings include the failure threshold, the sliding window length for counting failures, the open state timeout, and the number of allowed test requests during half-open. If you set the threshold too low, you risk false positives where transient hiccups open the circuit unnecessarily. If the threshold is too high, the breaker will not protect callers soon enough. A sliding window helps you weight recent failures more heavily. Open timeouts should reflect expected recovery duration; very short timeouts can cause flapping between open and half-open states, while very long timeouts delay recovery checks. Sampling a limited number of test requests during half-open avoids overloading a recovering service. A common mistake is relying on defaults without observing real traffic patterns. Another is configuring fallbacks that are costly or reintroduce load. Use real metrics: track open events, fallback invocations, and recovery times. Start conservatively, observe, and iterate. Ask: do these settings reduce user impact in a real failure scenario or merely hide it? Tuning and common mistakes for circuit breakers means balance sensitivity and stability: use metrics to refine thresholds, timeouts, and sampling to avoid false opens and flapping.. In practical terms, choosing thresholds, timeouts, and half-open sampling correctly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Tune with metrics
keyIdea.text: Balance sensitivity and stability: use metrics to refine thresholds, timeouts, and sampling to avoid false opens and flapping.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Tuning & Mistakes
Key settings
  • Failure threshold and sliding window size.
  • Open timeout before attempting half-open.
  • Number of test requests in half-open.
  • Timeout per request to avoid long waits being counted as success.
Common mistakes
  • Using defaults without validating against real traffic.
  • Setting thresholds that cause false positives during short spikes.
  • Using costly fallbacks that reintroduce load.
  • Not instrumenting circuit events, so opens go unnoticed.
Key Takeaway

Tune based on observed errors and latency. Instrument opens and fallback usage so thresholds evolve from data, not guesswork.

screens.title: Bulkhead pattern
screens.subtitle: Partition resources to limit blast radius

narration.text: The Bulkhead pattern isolates resources used for different operations so a problem in one area does not exhaust capacity for others. The pattern draws its name from ship bulkheads: watertight compartments that contain flooding. In software, you might allocate separate thread pools or connection pools for calls to different downstream services. For instance, UserService could have one thread pool for ProfileService calls and another for AuthService calls. If ProfileService becomes slow and consumes its pool, AuthService calls can continue using its own pool and user logins remain functional. A common mistake is mis-sizing pools; too small and you starve functionality, too large and you waste resources while offering little protection. Another pitfall is sharing dependent resources like database connections across compartments, which defeats the isolation. Bulkheads are especially valuable for preserving critical flows while allowing non-critical operations to fail or degrade gracefully. The takeaway: partition resources where failure would otherwise cascade, and size compartments based on criticality and expected load. Bulkhead pattern means isolate capacity for different integrations so a failing dependency cannot exhaust shared resources and bring down unrelated features.. In practical terms, partition resources to limit blast radius. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Bulkhead core
keyIdea.text: Isolate capacity for different integrations so a failing dependency cannot exhaust shared resources and bring down unrelated features.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Bulkhead Pattern
Analogy
Watertight Compartments

Like a ship's bulkheads, software bulkheads contain failures in separate resource compartments so one breach doesn't sink the whole system.

Concrete example
Separate thread pools for ProfileService and AuthService calls; if ProfileService is slow, AuthService still operates.
Design guidance
  • Identify independent interaction classes to isolate.
  • Allocate pools sized by criticality and expected load.
  • Avoid sharing low-level resources across bulkheads that defeat isolation.
Pitfall

Misconfigured sizes either starve features or waste capacity; size based on observed usage and criticality.

screens.title: Implementing bulkheads: thread pools and resource limits
screens.subtitle: Concrete patterns for isolating resource usage

narration.text: Bulkheads are implemented by partitioning resources such as thread pools, connection pools, or queues for different integrations. One simple approach is to create dedicated executor services for critical downstream calls. For example, designate an executor for ProfileService requests and a separate executor for AuthService. If ProfileService becomes slow, its executor fills up and rejects new work or returns a controlled error, while the Auth executor remains unaffected. Another tactic is limiting outbound connection pools per integration. If possible, prefer bounded queues and fail-fast rejection policies to avoid unlimited backlog growth. A common misconception is to think bulkheads introduce complexity without benefit. While they add configuration, they significantly reduce incident blast radius and make recovery predictable. Instrument each bulkhead with metrics: pool usage, rejection counts, and queue depth. Those signals help you tune sizes and detect when a compartment needs adjustment. The takeaway: implement isolation using bounded resources and observe behavior under load to refine sizes and policies. Implementing bulkheads: thread pools and resource limits means use bounded executors and per-integration pools with rejection policies and metrics to observe and tune bulkheads.. In practical terms, concrete patterns for isolating resource usage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Implementation tip
keyIdea.text: Use bounded executors and per-integration pools with rejection policies and metrics to observe and tune bulkheads.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Bulkhead Implementation
Executor-based bulkheads
Create separate bounded executors for different downstream services and use rejection policies to avoid unbounded queues.
Example config
ProfileExecutor: core=5,max=10,queue=50. AuthExecutor: core=10,max=20,queue=200. Tune based on criticality.
Connection & queue isolation
Limit outbound connections per integration and use bounded queues with backpressure or rejection to prevent global exhaustion.
Operational guidance

Emit metrics for pool saturation and rejections so you know when to adjust sizes or route traffic differently.

Misconception check

Avoid sharing database connections across bulkheads; shared low-level resources can negate isolation benefits.

screens.title: Hands-on activity: OrderService & ShippingService
screens.subtitle: Apply circuit breaker logic and propose a fallback

narration.text: Let's apply the patterns conceptually to a concrete scenario. You have an OrderService that calls an unreliable ShippingService for rates. First, protect the call with a circuit breaker configured to detect repeated timeouts or 5xx errors. Define the actions in each state: in Closed, allow requests and count failures; if failures exceed a threshold, transition to Open. In Open, immediately return a fallback response such as a cached estimate or queue the rate lookup for asynchronous completion. After a configured timeout, transition to Half-Open and allow a small number of test requests. If those succeed, close the circuit; otherwise re-open. As a fallback strategy, prefer queuing the rate lookup and allowing order placement with a note that shipping will be confirmed later — this preserves revenue while deferring the unreliable call. Common mistakes here would be using an overly small half-open sample or a fallback that also calls ShippingService. Instrument all transitions and fallback invocations so you can tune thresholds and observe user impact. Now write the state actions and fallback you would use for your own OrderService, and consider metrics you'll monitor to validate the design.

keyIdea.title: Activity goal
keyIdea.text: Design state actions and an independent fallback for OrderService calling ShippingService, then choose metrics to validate behavior.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Activity: OrderService
Template: Circuit Breaker Application
Use this outline to fill in your design.
Closed
Action: Allow requests; count failures. Transition condition: failures > threshold in sliding window.
Open
Action: Immediately return fallback or queue request. Transition condition: timeout elapsed.
Half-Open
Action: Allow limited test requests. Transition: close on success; re-open on failure.
Suggested fallback
Queue the shipping rate lookup for async processing and accept the order with a note that shipping will be confirmed. Optionally return a cached estimate for immediate user feedback.
Monitoring
Track circuit open events, fallback invocations, queue backlog, and half-open test success rates to tune thresholds and detect regressions.
Check your understanding

Write the transition conditions and the exact fallback action for your OrderService. Would the fallback preserve customer experience and keep system resources bounded?

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential concepts to remember. Resilience is the discipline of designing systems that continue to operate, possibly in degraded mode, when components fail. Cascading failures happen when one failure causes dependent services to struggle, and containment prevents this propagation. The Circuit Breaker pattern detects repeated failures and stops calls to a failing service, then probes for recovery using a Half-Open state. Fallback methods are the planned degraded behaviors invoked when the circuit is open; they should be independent and bounded in resource usage. The Bulkhead pattern isolates resources into compartments so a slow dependency cannot exhaust capacity for unrelated operations. Together, circuit breakers and bulkheads reduce blast radius and give teams time to fix root causes while keeping critical functionality available. Always combine these patterns with monitoring and logging so you can observe when they trigger and tune parameters based on real traffic patterns. Which single metric would you monitor first to know these patterns are helping your service?

keyIdea.title: Compact summary
keyIdea.text: Use circuit breakers to stop futile calls and bulkheads to isolate resource consumption; instrument both to guide tuning.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Key Concepts
Resilience
The system's ability to recover and continue functioning, possibly in degraded mode.
Circuit Breaker
Stops calling a failing service after repeated errors and probes for recovery with test requests.
Bulkhead
Isolates resources into compartments so one slow dependency doesn't exhaust global capacity.
Final takeaway

Combine containment patterns with monitoring and fallbacks to reduce incident impact and buy time for root cause fixes.

narration.text: Keep three practical reminders at hand. First, treat failures as expected, not exceptional; design timeouts and retries with backoff and limits. Second, use a circuit breaker to stop futile repeated calls and provide a fallback so callers behave predictably during outages. Third, use bulkheads to partition resources so a slow integration cannot exhaust pools needed by other features. For each reminder, instrument events and metrics so you know when a pattern is active and whether its configuration is helping. These three practices — expect failure, stop futile calls, and partition resources — are the foundation for resilient microservices. As you leave this chapter, pick one dependency to protect and implement either a circuit breaker with a reasonable fallback or a bulkhead with metrics to validate the choice. What to Remember means expect failure, stop futile repeats, partition resources; always monitor and iterate based on real data.. In practical terms, three compact concept cards. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › What to Remember
Expect Failures
Design timeouts and bounded retries as a first line of defense.
Stop Repeats
Use circuit breakers and meaningful fallbacks to avoid wasting resources.
Partition Resources
Use bulkheads to contain resource usage per integration and avoid global exhaustion.
Final action

Pick one dependency, add a circuit breaker or bulkhead, instrument it, and iterate based on the metrics you observe.
